newsitem.title: NORWAY: Statoil sees improved oil recovery at Gullfaks.
newsitem.headline: Statoil sees improved oil recovery at Gullfaks.

text.p: Twice the oil originally forecast could be recovered from Norwegian North Sea block 34/10, which includes the main Gullfaks development, operator Den norske stats oljeselskap AS said on Thursday.
Under a new long-term plan for the area, the Gullfaks field will be assured profitable operation until 2012, Statoil's Status Weekly newsletter said.

Gullfaks celebrates 10 years of production on December 22 when the Gullfaks A platform started up in 1986. The B platform began production in February 1988, with Gullfaks C following in November 1989.

Statoil said a total 1.9 billion barrels of oil could be recovered from the main field compared with original estimates of 1.3 billion. With satellites and expected new discoveries, up to 2.7 billion barrels could be recovered, it said.

The company said it planned to concentrate on improving recovery rate as well as continued exploration and development. Statoil hopes to raise the recovery factor for the main field to 60 percent, while planned recovery for the satellites is 40 percent.

Remaining recoverable reserves in Gullfaks were estimated at about 1.5 billion barrels. The target for 2000 is to produce 78 percent of the volume achieved in the peak year of 1994 -- around 150 million barrels on an annual basis, Statoil said.

The field set a daily production record of 606,000 barrels of oil on October 7, 1994, the same year as it hit peak annual output of 193 million barrels. Gullfaks is expected to pump 152 million barrels in 1996.

"The Gullfaks South, Rimfaks and Gullveig satellites, due on stream in 1998, will make a significant contribution to keeping output at this level," Arild Hesjedal, petroleum technology manager for Gullfaks, told the newsletter.
The satellites will be tied back to the Gullfaks A installation.

Statoil said it planned to simplify operation of Gullfaks B platform to bring operating costs in line with lower production. The company will reduce staff at the platform from 1998 and will eventually operate it as a remotely-operated wellhead unit.
